questions.question: What is the difference between adult and child CPR?
questions.solution_html:
• The main difference between adult and child CPR lies in the technique and sequence of actions.
  • For a child, use one of your hands. Place the heel of the hand at their sternum, which is in the
  • center of the chest, between and slightly below their nipples. Press down hard and fast around 1.5
  • inches deep, or one-third the depth of the chest. For an infant, use two fingers. Place your fingers
  • in the center of their chest, between and slightly below the nipples. For adults, place the heel of
  • one hand in the middle of the chest. Place your other hand on top of the first hand and interlace
  • the fingers. For adults, compress the chest to a depth of at least 2 inches. Rescue breaths follow
  • the same ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths for both adults and children
questions.final_answer: the same ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths for both adults and children
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) Regular Exam Sem 1, Nov 2024

questions.question: Why should the bleeding injury elevate above the heart level?
questions.solution_html:
• Elevating a bleeding injury above heart level is a first-aid technique used to help control bleeding.
  • By elevating the injured area above the heart, gravity reduces the blood pressure in the blood
  • vessels at the injury site, making it harder for blood to flow out of the wound. This reduces the
  • stress on the heart. Slower blood flow allows the natural clotting. Elevation also helps to reduce
  • swelling in the injured area.
questions.final_answer: swelling in the injured area

questions.question: Describe the main objectives of first aid. How do these objectives helps in save lives?
questions.solution_html:
• First aid is the act of providing immediate assistance to someone who is injured or suddenly
  • becomes ill. The goal is to support recovery and keep the situation from getting worse until
  • professional medical help is available. The main objectives of first aid are often summarized as
  • the "Three Ps."
  • Preserve Life: The main purpose of first aid is to prevent the condition from worsening. This
  • could include performing life-saving techniques such as CPR.
  • Prevent Further Injury/Illness: This includes steps to avoid further injuries or conditions, such
  • as stabilizing a person's condition or preventing an infection.
  • Promote Recovery: After immediate threats are managed, first aiders can help begin the
  • recovery process by ensuring the person is comfortable and secure until further help arrives
questions.final_answer: recovery process by ensuring the person is comfortable and secure until further help arrives

questions.question: What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary muscles?
questions.solution_html:
• Muscles in the human body can be classified into voluntary and involuntary muscles based on
  • whether their movement is under conscious control. Voluntary muscles are under our conscious
  • control and are responsible for body movements like walking, lifting, and running. Skeletal
  • Muscles are voluntary muscles and striated in appearance due to organized muscle fibers.
  • Involuntary muscles are not under our conscious control and contract and relax automatically.
  • They are also known as unstriated or smooth muscles. Smooth Muscles are found in the walls of
  • internal organs (e.g., stomach, intestines, and blood vessels). Cardiac Muscles are found only in
  • the heart. Involuntary, works automatically to maintain the heartbeat.
questions.final_answer: the heart. Involuntary, works automatically to maintain the heartbeat

questions.question: What are the signs that someone might need CPR?
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: Unresponsive, not breathing or gasping, no pulse.
  • A person may need CPR when they are completely unresponsive and do not react to
  • calling or tapping. They may not be breathing at all, or they may only gasp weakly
  • which is not normal breathing. Their chest will not rise and fall normally. They may also
  • have no pulse or signs of circulation. In such situations, the person’s heart and breathing
  • have stopped, and CPR must be started immediately to keep blood and oxygen flowing
  • until medical help arrives.
questions.final_answer: until medical help arrives

questions.question: Explain the concept of high-quality CPR and its components.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: 100–120 compressions/min, proper depth, full recoil, minimal interruptions
  • good ventilation.
  • High-quality CPR means giving chest compressions and breaths in the most effective
  • way to increase the person’s chance of survival. It includes pushing hard and fast at a rate
  • of 100–120 compressions per minute and pressing deep enough to help blood flow. The
  • chest should be allowed to come back fully after each compression. There should be very
  • few interruptions, and breaths should be given gently so the chest rises without over
  • ventilating. Using an AED as soon as possible is also part of good CPR practice. All
  • these components together help maintain the flow of oxygen to the heart and brain.
questions.final_answer: these components together help maintain the flow of oxygen to the heart and brain
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Describe the steps involved in providing first aid to a person with shock?
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: Lay them down, elevate legs, keep warm, control bleeding, monitor breathing
  • and call emergency help.
  • When giving first aid for shock, the first aider should quickly call for medical help and
  • keep the person lying down. The legs can be raised slightly to improve blood flow to vital
  • organs, unless there is a suspected injury that prevents it. The person should be kept
  • warm using a blanket to prevent further heat loss. Any visible bleeding must be
  • controlled immediately by applying pressure. The first aider should stay calm, reassure
  • the person, and monitor their breathing and response. Nothing should be given to eat or
  • drink, and the person must not be moved unnecessarily. These steps help maintain
  • circulation and prevent the condition from getting worse.
questions.final_answer: circulation and prevent the condition from getting worse
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: What is the difference between adult and child CPR?
questions.solution_html:
• The main difference between adult and child CPR lies in the technique and sequence of actions.
  • For a child, use one of your hands. Place the heel of the hand at their sternum, which is in the
  • center of the chest, between and slightly below their nipples. Press down hard and fast around 1.5
  • inches deep, or one-third the depth of the chest. For an infant, use two fingers. Place your fingers
  • in the center of their chest, between and slightly below the nipples. For adults, place the heel of
  • one hand in the middle of the chest. Place your other hand on top of the first hand and interlace
  • the fingers. For adults, compress the chest to a depth of at least 2 inches. Rescue breaths follow
  • the same ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths for both adults and children
questions.final_answer: the same ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths for both adults and children

questions.question: Why should the bleeding injury elevate above the heart level?
questions.solution_html:
• Elevating a bleeding injury above heart level is a first-aid technique used to help control bleeding.
  • By elevating the injured area above the heart, gravity reduces the blood pressure in the blood
  • vessels at the injury site, making it harder for blood to flow out of the wound. This reduces the
  • stress on the heart. Slower blood flow allows the natural clotting. Elevation also helps to reduce
  • swelling in the injured area.
questions.final_answer: swelling in the injured area

questions.question: Describe the main objectives of first aid. How do these objectives helps in save lives?
questions.solution_html:
• First aid is the act of providing immediate assistance to someone who is injured or suddenly
  • becomes ill. The goal is to support recovery and keep the situation from getting worse until
  • professional medical help is available. The main objectives of first aid are often summarized as
  • the "Three Ps."
  • Preserve Life: The main purpose of first aid is to prevent the condition from worsening. This
  • could include performing life-saving techniques such as CPR.
  • Prevent Further Injury/Illness: This includes steps to avoid further injuries or conditions, such
  • as stabilizing a person's condition or preventing an infection.
  • Promote Recovery: After immediate threats are managed, first aiders can help begin the
  • recovery process by ensuring the person is comfortable and secure until further help arrives
questions.final_answer: recovery process by ensuring the person is comfortable and secure until further help arrives

questions.question: What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary muscles?

  • whether their movement is under conscious control. Voluntary muscles are under our conscious
  • control and are responsible for body movements like walking, lifting, and running. Skeletal
  • Muscles are voluntary muscles and striated in appearance due to organized muscle fibers.
  • Involuntary muscles are not under our conscious control and contract and relax automatically.
  • They are also known as unstriated or smooth muscles. Smooth Muscles are found in the walls of
  • internal organs (e.g., stomach, intestines, and blood vessels). Cardiac Muscles are found only in
  • the heart. Involuntary, works automatically to maintain the heartbeat.
questions.final_answer: the heart. Involuntary, works automatically to maintain the heartbeat

questions.question: What are the signs that someone might need CPR?

  • which is not normal breathing. Their chest will not rise and fall normally. They may also

questions.question: Explain the concept of high-quality CPR and its components.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: 100–120 compressions/min, proper depth, full recoil, minimal interruptions
  • good ventilation.
  • High-quality CPR means giving chest compressions and breaths in the most effective
  • way to increase the person’s chance of survival. It includes pushing hard and fast at a rate
  • of 100–120 compressions per minute and pressing deep enough to help blood flow. The
  • chest should be allowed to come back fully after each compression. There should be very
  • few interruptions, and breaths should be given gently so the chest rises without over
  • ventilating. Using an AED as soon as possible is also part of good CPR practice. All
  • these components together help maintain the flow of oxygen to the heart and brain.
questions.final_answer: these components together help maintain the flow of oxygen to the heart and brain

questions.question: Describe the steps involved in providing first aid to a person with shock?
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: Lay them down, elevate legs, keep warm, control bleeding, monitor breathing
  • and call emergency help.
  • When giving first aid for shock, the first aider should quickly call for medical help and
  • keep the person lying down. The legs can be raised slightly to improve blood flow to vital
  • organs, unless there is a suspected injury that prevents it. The person should be kept
  • warm using a blanket to prevent further heat loss. Any visible bleeding must be
  • controlled immediately by applying pressure. The first aider should stay calm, reassure
  • the person, and monitor their breathing and response. Nothing should be given to eat or
  • drink, and the person must not be moved unnecessarily. These steps help maintain
  • circulation and prevent the condition from getting worse.
questions.final_answer: circulation and prevent the condition from getting worse
